title: Taking the light

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hari, called on in the arti song, Om jai jagadish hare. Your line was victory to the lord of the world. Did you start with thanks before asking for anything? Day one hundred and twenty-one.
screen: `OM JAI JAGADISH HARE — VICTORY TO THE LORD OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The first time you go to arti with a Hindu friend, there's a moment that can catch you off guard. The song ends. The bell stops. And then the person holding the lamp turns around and walks toward you, holding out the plate with the flame still burning. Everyone near you does something with their hands, quickly, easily, like they've done it all their lives. And you stand there wondering: am I supposed to touch it? Blow on it? Pass? Today, the moment after the song: taking the light.
screen: `THE SONG ENDS.` → `THE PLATE COMES TOWARD YOU.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH YOUR HANDS?`

segments.voice: Here's what people are doing. When the arti plate reaches you, you cup your hands and pass them over the flame, close enough to feel the warmth, never touching. Then you draw your hands back toward yourself and bring them to your eyes, your face, sometimes over the top of your head. Some do it twice or three times. Some use both hands. Some use only the right. That's it. It takes about three seconds. Why? The idea is simple. The flame has just been circled before the divine. It has been, you might say, in the presence. Now it comes out to the people, and you take a little of that light and warmth and bring it into yourself: over the eyes, so you see well; over the head, as a blessing. Remember your fourteenth word, arti, and its line, light passed hand to hand. This is that line, literally. The light went to the shrine, and now it goes from palm to palm through the whole room. A few quiet customs travel with it. An arti flame usually isn't blown out; blowing on a sacred flame is often seen as disrespectful, so it's left to burn down or put out another way. In temples, people often drop a coin or a small note on the plate as it passes. And if you're a guest and unsure, it's fine to watch first, then copy the person next to you. Nobody is keeping score. The light is offered to everyone in the room.
screen: `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, NOT TOUCHING.` · `BACK TO THE EYES, THE FACE, THE HEAD.` · `LIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `DON'T BLOW IT OUT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or lamp and it's safe, light it and set it steady in front of you. If not, picture the arti plate coming toward you. Cup your hands. Pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching. Draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes. Feel the warmth there. Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head. Then rest your hands in your lap and stay with the flame. The bell holds the time.
Jyoti, the flame: after arti, hands pass over it and come back to the eyes and the head, taking the shrine's light into yourself. Today's word.
Your line: take it. Today, when something good is offered to you, a compliment, help, a kindness, don't wave it away. Take it. Day one hundred and twenty-one.

howItsDone: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.

original.note: Sanskrit jyoti: light, flame. The light people take from the arti plate.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hand gesture everyone seems to know.
what it means: taking the light that was circled before the divine and bringing it to your eyes and head, as a blessing.

what a scholar hears: receiving the arti flame makes the rite reciprocal: light offered to the deity returns to the worshipper, like prasad from the food offering; it's also why arti is remembered as 'light passed hand to hand'.
